Resolves #18138

Circular reveals now own both snapshot layers: the old state stays opaque outside the growing circle, and normal blending replaces the browser cross-fade for that reveal. The engine releases its generated effects when the transition settles. Portal and Workstation no longer need global cancellation CSS; raw animations and the immediate Boolean return keep their existing behavior.

Evidence: L3 (native Chrome compositing, pixels, lifecycle controls, and visible app theme clicks) → L3 required (AC-1–5). No residuals.

## AC Evidence

| AC | Evidence |
|---|---|
| AC-1 | Outside-CI: `ViewTransitionReveal.spec.mjs` samples the real engine method halfway through the reveal after the UA fade; screenshot pixels are new blue inside the circle and old red outside. |
| AC-2 | Outside-CI: the same browser spec observes natural completion, cancelled generated handles, and a subsequent plain transition with fractional opacity and UA `plus-lighter` blending. |
| AC-3 | Outside-CI: [intake measurement](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/issues/18138#issuecomment-5547601549) records the visible Chrome 152 precedence control; the permanent browser spec enforces both layers' opacity/blending. |
| AC-4 | Both SCSS rules and the obsolete Workstation explanation are removed. Visible theme-click probes in both apps found zero loaded old/new cancellation rules and two released engine effects. |
| AC-5 | Outside-CI: rendered frames from actual Portal and Workstation theme controls were inspected at 300ms and after completion in visible Chrome 152. Workstation retains the dark state outside the light circle; Portal retains its complete backdrop/header. Both snapshot opacities were 1 with normal blending. |

## Deltas from ticket

The JS candidate passed the browser gate. Filled effects last until the transition settles, including zero/short reveals; partial registration failure unwinds already-created effects. The browser regression also runs in current headless Chrome, beyond the previous harness limitation.

Integration hygiene: lowers the existing dock Workspace size baseline from 1419 to its measured 1415 lines after merged #18329, so this PR does not inherit a stale-baseline guard failure. No dock runtime change.

## Test Evidence

`npx playwright test -c test/playwright/playwright.config.e2e.mjs test/playwright/e2e/rendering/ViewTransitionReveal.spec.mjs`: ten native-browser cases pass in both default headless mode and with `--headed`, including unassisted completion, zero/80ms durations, skipped/failed registration, raw payload priority and unrelated-animation preservation. Before implementation, the two new helper assertions failed on the missing old-layer descriptor and fill behavior.

### 🧭 Patch-Blind Premise Snapshot

*   **Inputs Read Before Patch:** #18138 (intent authority — its census, Architectural Reality, and preferred JS direction); the changed-file list; current `dev` source of `src/main/DomAccess.mjs` + `src/main/DomUtils.mjs`; the two consumer stylesheets being emptied; and a prior-art sweep that surfaced my own 2026-08-24 session on this exact surface (Chrome view-transition regression) plus the 2026-01 sessions that established the `delay` time-window pattern. Not the PR body as primary premise.
*   **Expected Solution Shape:** The engine registers old-layer compositing **only when a reveal is actually running**, so a caller with no `reveal` keeps the UA cross-fade. The boundary it must NOT hardcode is duration/easing duplicated across the two layers — two copies drift, and the old layer outliving or undershooting the new one reproduces the same black frame from the other side. Test isolation should include an arm proving the **no-reveal** path registers nothing.
*   **Patch Verdict:** **Matches, and closes an edge I arrived with.** `oldLayer` is nested inside the new-layer payload, so `createRevealAnimation() === null` yields no companion by construction — the UA path cannot be poisoned. `options` is built once and spread into both layers, so drift is structurally impossible rather than merely avoided. My prior-art falsifier was sharper: my 2026-08-24 session recorded `ViewportController` declaring `radius, x, y` with no fallbacks, so a falsy `clientX` produced `circle(0px at undefinedpx undefinedpx)` — invalid, dropped, UA fade. Under this diff, an *undefined* coordinate with a valid `oldLayer` would have held the old layer opaque with nothing revealing behind it: a frozen screen, worse than the black one. The guard at `DomUtils.mjs:87` uses `== null`, which catches `undefined` as well as `null`, so that path returns `null` and never reaches `oldLayer`. Verified at exact head, not inferred from the comment.
*   **Premise Coherence:** Coheres with friction→gold and with the engine-owns-the-primitive value: two consumers, one undocumented idiom, one black-screen ship — the response is a primitive, not a doc line. The `console.warn` block is the clearest instance: it states what it can detect and explicitly names what it cannot ("a reveal that registers and then rasterises wrongly … stays invisible to every runtime signal this method can read"), which is verify-before-assert applied to the author's own instrument.

### 🔬 Depth Floor

**Challenge:** The pixel arm asserts exact RGBA equality — `toEqual([[20, 80, 220, 255], [200, 30, 40, 255]])`. That exactness is what makes it a real black-screen witness, and I would not trade it for a tolerance. But it is also the assertion most likely to fail opaquely on a future runner image, a different GPU/driver, or any antialiasing that reaches the sample points; the failure would read as "colour changed", not "the old layer stopped being held". Worth knowing that the sample coordinates' distance from the circle edge is load-bearing, so a later change to the reveal's radius maths could brush a sample point without anyone connecting the two.

**Rhetorical-Drift Audit:**

- [x] PR description: the `Evidence: L3 … → L3 required (AC-1–5). No residuals.` line matches what the suite substantiates — native Chrome compositing with real pixel reads, not a payload proxy.
- [x] Anchor & Echo summaries: precise. "Filled effects must be cancelled when the owning view transition settles, not when their duration elapses" is a durable rule, not a snapshot anchor, and it is the exact behaviour `transition.finished.then(cleanup, cleanup)` implements.
- [x] `[RETROSPECTIVE]`: none claimed; no inflation to audit.
- [x] Linked anchors: #18136/#18137 genuinely establish the second-consumer census the premise rests on.

**Findings:** Pass. One note rather than drift — the `??`-vs-`||` comment lost its cross-link to the sibling class ("the same class of bug as reading `x: 0` as no coordinate") when the block moved up into `options`. The surviving one-liner keeps the rule; the link that made it memorable is gone.

### 📊 Evaluation Metrics

*   **`[ARCH_ALIGNMENT]`**: 95 — the capability lands in the realm that already owns the animation, both consumer stylesheets lose the obligation, and the raw-`data.animate` boundary is preserved explicitly rather than by omission. 5 deducted because the return shape is asymmetric: the new layer is the object and the old layer is a nested `oldLayer` companion, so a reader meets `{keyframes, options, oldLayer: {keyframes, options}}` where `{newLayer, oldLayer}` would read as two peers of one transition.
*   **`[CONTENT_COMPLETENESS]`**: 96 — `@param` covers `duration`, `easing`, `x`, `y`; the percentage-units rationale, the cancellation-timing rule and the nullish-default reasoning are all anchored, and the `@returns` tag moved with the contract. 4 deducted for the one prose loss noted above: the `??` comment's cross-link to the sibling `x: 0` bug did not survive the move into `options`.
*   **`[EXECUTION_QUALITY]`**: 96 — `finished.then(cleanup, cleanup)` is attached before `ready` can resolve, so there is no window where the transition settles unobserved; `effects` is a per-invocation closure, so cleanup cannot reach another transition's animations; the coordinate guard catches `undefined` and the zero-viewport case is guarded separately with its reasoning recorded. 4 deducted only for the brittleness noted in the Challenge, which is a property of the strongest arm rather than of the engine code.
*   **`[PRODUCTIVITY]`**: 100 — the ticket's preferred direction implemented as specified, with both consumer rules deleted in the same change rather than left for a follow-up.
*   **`[IMPACT]`**: 80 — converts a half-primitive into a whole one on a core main-thread surface and removes an undocumented obligation that had already shipped one black screen; consumer #3 now cannot hit it.
*   **`[COMPLEXITY]`**: 65 — small diff, but it reasons across two realms at once (view-transition pseudo-element compositing and the transition lifecycle), and the correctness argument depends on promise-settlement order rather than on the visible control flow.
*   **`[EFFORT_PROFILE]`**: Quick Win — contained engine change with a large correctness gain; the bulk of the diff is the 245-line suite that makes the gain checkable rather than asserted.

Nothing here needs changing. The part I would keep and reuse is the pixel arm's in-test control: when the defect is an absence, an arm that only proves your effects were registered cannot tell "restored" from "never ran", and this one asserts the UA's own `plus-lighter` back into place to close that gap.
